title: 'His memories are alive in all of us': Man identified in fatal police shooting inside northern Ontario courtroom
subtitle: The incident has drawn attention to what lawyers say are the "woefully inadequate" security measures at so-called fly-in courts.
article: The man fatally shot by police inside a makeshift northern Ontario courtroom that was in session last Thursday has been identified as 23-year-old Tyresse Kenny Padro Cree Roundsky.

As the Star first reported last week , the man was reportedly able to get between the defence counsel's and judge's tables at the fly-in court in Wapekeka First Nation with what police say was a knife, before he was shot by an OPP officer. The Special Investigations Unit is now probing the incident.
"His memories are alive in all of us," said a brief statement from Wapekeka First Nation.
The press release indicated that Roundsky is survived by his grandparents, sister and her children, his main caregiver, "and by many families and friends and the youth of Wapekeka First Nation."

The incident has drawn attention to what lawyers say are the "woefully inadequate" security measures at so-called fly-in courts , which are temporary courtrooms set up in public buildings like schools and community centres in remote communities, with the judge, lawyers and staff flying in from elsewhere. For instance, there are no metal detectors, and officers are also not equipped with wands to search people for possible weapons. The fly-in court last week in Wapekeka was set up in a youth centre.

"The security measures at this fly-in court, and many other fly-in courts in our northern communities, are woefully inadequate. This has been a reality for decades," said Donna Kellway, president of the Ontario Crown Attorneys' Association, in an email to prosecutors last Friday obtained by the Star.
She said her association had warned the Ontario government for years about "deficiencies" and "unacceptable shortcomings" in courthouse security.

"Those deficiencies are particularly glaring in our northern communities," Kellway wrote. "Our concerns have not been adequately addressed, and that is clearer today than it has ever been. Rest assured that we will not sit idly by in the wake of this chilling incident."

The incident prompted Ontario Court Chief Justice Sharon Nicklas to call for an emergency meeting on courthouse security with Attorney General Doug Downey and others, which was expected to take place Tuesday.

"Our thoughts are with the loved ones of the deceased, the Wapekeka First Nation and its members, and those who were in the courtroom today," Nicklas wrote in an email to colleagues last week that was obtained by the Star.
